idiom_name: Django @cache_page / CacheMiddleware over the configured CACHES backend
implementation_notes: Django's per-view cache is a page cache: @cache_page(60 * 5) on a view, or CacheMiddleware with CACHE_MIDDLEWARE_SECONDS for the whole site, stores the rendered response in the backend configured under CACHES - memcached, Redis or the filesystem backend - and serves it without calling the view at all; vary_on_cookie/vary_on_headers and CACHE_MIDDLEWARE_KEY_PREFIX carry the Vary axes, and client request directives such as no-cache/no-store are honoured by the middleware. The backend is the real decision: LocMemCache is per-process (fine for one worker, misleading behind several), while memcached/Redis give one shared cache that survives restarts. It replaces the hand-written store completely, but the view must still be pure with respect to the key - anything it reads outside the key is frozen into the entry.
pitfalls: The default LocMemCache is per process: with several gunicorn workers the same page lives in several caches and a purge reaches only one of them - configure memcached/Redis before relying on hits.
Without vary_on_cookie/vary_on_headers (or an explicit Vary on the response) a page rendered for a logged-in user is stored under the plain URL and served to everyone.
Caching a view that writes messages or session state stores those values in a shared entry; keep per-request state out of cached views or strip it before the response is cached.

variants.name: Django per-view cache (@cache_page / CacheMiddleware)
In-process render memoisation (functools.cache / lru_cache)
variants.implementation_notes: When the page body is a pure function of a few hashable parameters and a single process serves the traffic, the page cache can be the renderer's own memo: @functools.cache (Python 3.9+) or @lru_cache(maxsize=...) keeps the returned body in the process and skips the rendering on repeat calls, which realizes 'serve it pre-generated' with no cache backend at all. It is valid only while the function is deterministic - no database reads outside the key, no clock, no session - and it is per-process with no TTL, so a deploy invalidates everything and a stale entry survives until eviction or restart. Move to the cache_page variant as soon as several workers must agree on freshness, a purge API is needed, or the page depends on anything outside the function's arguments.
pitfalls: Hits return the same object to every caller: immutable strings are safe, but returning a list or dict means all requests share one mutable value.
There is no TTL and no per-key expiry - functools.cache grows until the process ends or you clear it, so a key built from user-supplied slugs is an unbounded memory leak.
Arguments are the cache key: passing unhashable or irrelevant values (request objects, ORM rows) either raises or destroys the hit rate, and per-request data silently makes the cache useless.
